items.prompt: In a team meeting, a frustrated coworker loudly blames you for a missed deadline that was not entirely your fault. Everyone turns to see how you will react. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 15:1?
options: Answer calmly and gently, acknowledging the frustration and offering to work out the problem together
Raise your voice to match theirs so everyone knows you will not be pushed around
List every mistake the coworker has made this quarter to put them in their place
Make a sarcastic remark that gets a laugh from the room at their expense
items.explanation: Proverbs 15:1 teaches that "a soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." A gentle reply calms the situation, while harsh or cutting words make it worse.
items.hint: The verse contrasts two kinds of answers and what each one does to anger.

items.prompt: A friend asks whether you liked the business plan they emailed you. You found serious problems in it, and a quick 'It's great!' would be much easier. What does Ephesians 4:25 counsel here?
options: Tell them it is perfect so you avoid an awkward conversation
Speak the truth to them kindly, because you are connected to one another
Say nothing and simply stop replying to their messages
Praise it to their face but tell others what you really think
items.explanation: Ephesians 4:25 says, "putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another." Honest speech, not a convenient falsehood, is the instruction.
items.hint: The verse gives a reason for honesty based on how believers are joined together.

items.prompt: A close colleague confides that they are struggling with a personal matter and asks you to keep it private. Later, over lunch, others start guessing about why the colleague seems distracted. According to Proverbs 11:13, what should you do?
options: Share what you know so the group understands and can be sympathetic
Drop hints without saying it outright, so you technically keep the secret
Keep the matter to yourself, as a person of a faithful spirit would
Reveal it only to the one coworker you trust most
items.explanation: Proverbs 11:13 contrasts the talebearer who "revealeth secrets" with one "of a faithful spirit" who "concealeth the matter." Keeping the confidence is the faithful choice.
items.hint: The verse contrasts two kinds of people by what they do with secrets.

items.prompt: A client keeps asking whether you will really deliver on Friday. You are tempted to pile on dramatic assurances like 'I swear on everything I have' to sound more convincing. Which approach best reflects Matthew 5:37?
options: Use the strongest guarantees you can think of so the client feels secure
Give a plain, honest 'yes' or 'no' and let your word stand on its own
Promise Friday now and quietly plan to explain later if it slips
Avoid giving any clear answer so you cannot be held to it
items.explanation: In Matthew 5:37 Jesus says, "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil." A simple, truthful answer is what He teaches.
items.hint: Jesus describes how plain a trustworthy answer should be.

items.prompt: Months ago, during a moving worship service, you made a sincere vow to God to give a specific gift to a ministry. Now money is tighter and you keep postponing it, thinking that perhaps the vow does not really count. What does Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 counsel?
options: Fulfil what you vowed without delay, since it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay
Consider the vow cancelled because circumstances have changed
Keep postponing indefinitely, since God does not mind delays
Make a larger vow to make up for the unpaid one
items.explanation: Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 says, "When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it... Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay." A vow should be kept, and kept promptly.
items.hint: The passage speaks both about timing and about whether vowing at all is wise.

items.prompt: Two family members are feuding, and each one calls you to vent about the other and pass along what was said. You notice the conflict grows every time comments get relayed between them. Which response best reflects Proverbs 26:20?
options: Pass along each side's remarks accurately so both stay informed
Refuse to carry stories between them, letting the quarrel lose its fuel
Tell each person the other said worse things than they did, to speed up a showdown
Post about the feud online to get outside opinions
items.explanation: Proverbs 26:20 says, "Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth." Refusing to carry tales removes the fuel that keeps strife burning.
items.hint: Think about what happens to a fire when no more wood is added.

items.prompt: You agreed to sell your car to a neighbour at a set price and shook hands on it. Before the transfer, someone else offers you considerably more. Which response best reflects the character described in Psalms 15:4?
options: Accept the higher offer, since nothing has been signed yet
Tell the neighbour they must match the new price or lose the deal
Keep your word to the neighbour even though it now costs you
Invent a mechanical problem so you can back out gracefully
items.explanation: Psalms 15:4 describes the one who may dwell with the LORD as "He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not." Such a person keeps a commitment even when it becomes costly.
items.hint: The psalm praises someone whose promise holds even when keeping it hurts.

items.prompt: A friend tells you a convincing story about how a mutual acquaintance cheated them, and you feel ready to share it and take sides. You have not heard from the other person at all. What does Proverbs 18:17 counsel here?
options: Recognize that the first account can seem right until the other side is examined, and withhold judgment
Trust the first account fully, since a friend would not mislead you
Warn others about the acquaintance right away to protect them
Confront the acquaintance publicly so the truth comes out quickly
items.explanation: Proverbs 18:17 says, "He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him." A one-sided story can sound right until it is examined, so judgment and repetition should wait.
items.hint: The verse notes how a case can appear before anyone questions it.

batch.theme: honest speech, gossip and keeping promises

items.prompt: A frustrated customer calls your desk and starts shouting about a billing mistake that wasn't your fault. You feel your own temper rising. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 15:1?
options: Raise your voice to match theirs so they know you won't be pushed around
Answer calmly and gently while you work toward a solution
Point out sharply that the mistake was someone else's fault
Hang up and let them call back when they've cooled off
items.explanation: Proverbs 15:1 teaches that 'a soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger,' so a gentle reply calms the conflict.
items.hint: This verse contrasts two kinds of answers and what each one does to anger.

items.prompt: You and your spouse had a heated disagreement about household chores after dinner. It's getting late, and you're tempted to go to bed still fuming and deal with it 'someday.' What does Ephesians 4:26 counsel here?
options: Let the anger simmer for a few days so the other person learns a lesson
Pretend nothing happened and never bring the issue up again
Deal with your anger promptly rather than letting it carry on unresolved
Sleep in another room until the other person apologizes first
items.explanation: Ephesians 4:26 says, 'Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath,' urging that anger be dealt with quickly rather than nursed.
items.hint: The verse uses the end of the day as a time marker for anger.

items.prompt: In a team meeting, a coworker criticizes a project you led. Before they finish explaining, you're already forming a sharp rebuttal in your head. Which response best reflects James 1:19-20?
options: Listen carefully to the full concern before answering, and keep your anger in check
Interrupt immediately so the criticism doesn't spread to others
Respond with a forceful counterattack to show you're confident
Stay silent in the meeting, then vent angrily about them afterward
items.explanation: James 1:19-20 calls us to be 'swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath,' because 'the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.'
items.hint: James lists three things to be quick or slow about, in a specific order.

items.prompt: You're heading to a worship service, ready to give an offering, when you remember that a friend is still hurt by a harsh comment you made last week. What does Jesus teach in Matthew 5:23-24?
options: Give a larger offering to make up for the harsh comment
Go and seek to be reconciled with your friend as a priority
Wait for your friend to come to you, since they're the one upset
Focus only on your worship; relationships are a separate matter
items.explanation: In Matthew 5:23-24 Jesus says to leave the gift, 'first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.'
items.hint: Jesus tells the worshipper what to do before offering at the altar.

items.prompt: A neighbor spread false rumors about you in your community group. Later you learn that their family has fallen on hard times and is struggling to afford groceries. Which response best reflects Romans 12:17-21?
options: Share the news of their hardship in the group so they feel what you felt
Ignore them entirely, since they brought this on themselves
Quietly work to get them removed from the community group
Refuse to take revenge and instead offer practical help, like food
items.explanation: Romans 12:19-21 says 'avenge not yourselves' and 'if thine enemy hunger, feed him,' concluding, 'overcome evil with good.'
items.hint: Paul describes what to do if an enemy is hungry or thirsty.

items.prompt: A minor disagreement with your sibling over splitting a restaurant bill is starting to escalate, and old grievances are creeping into the conversation. What does Proverbs 17:14 counsel here?
options: Bring up every past grievance now so everything is finally aired
Insist on settling the exact amount, no matter how long it takes
Drop the quarrel early, before it grows into something bigger
Keep arguing but lower your voice so it seems more reasonable
items.explanation: Proverbs 17:14 compares 'the beginning of strife' to letting out water, so we should 'leave off contention, before it be meddled with.'
items.hint: The verse compares a quarrel's start to a small breach that releases water.

items.prompt: Walking through the office, you overhear two colleagues from another department arguing over a matter that has nothing to do with you. You're tempted to jump in and tell them who's right. Which response best reflects Proverbs 26:17?
options: Stay out of a quarrel that doesn't belong to you
Step in and take a side, since you clearly know who's right
Report both of them to their manager to show initiative
Tell other coworkers about the argument so everyone's aware
items.explanation: Proverbs 26:17 says he 'that passeth by, and meddleth with strife belonging not to him, is like one that taketh a dog by the ears'—inviting needless trouble.
items.hint: The proverb uses a vivid picture involving an animal to describe interfering.

items.prompt: A friend tells you that someone at work grumbled about you behind your back. You feel stung and start planning to confront them over every word. Which response best reflects Ecclesiastes 7:21-22?
options: Track down exactly what was said so you can respond point by point
Don't dwell on every remark, remembering you have spoken against others too
Start grumbling about them too, so things are even
Ask your friend to keep reporting anything else said about you
items.explanation: Ecclesiastes 7:21-22 advises to 'take no heed unto all words that are spoken,' because 'thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others.'
items.hint: The Preacher appeals to your own conscience about your past words.

items.prompt: You have just landed the biggest client in your company's history, and you start telling coworkers that the team couldn't function without you. You feel untouchable and stop double-checking your work. Which attitude best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 16:18?
options: Recognize that a haughty spirit sets you up for a fall, and stay humble and careful
Enjoy the moment, because success shows that your pride is justified
Make sure everyone knows the win was yours before someone else claims it
Relax your standards, since past success guarantees future success
items.explanation: Proverbs 16:18 warns that "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall." Humility and care guard against the fall that pride invites.
items.hint: This verse links an inner attitude to an outcome that soon follows it.

items.prompt: You are planning to put most of your savings into a new business idea. A trusted friend with years of experience offers to review your plan, but you are already certain it will work. What does Proverbs 12:15 counsel here?
options: Decline the review, because confidence in your own judgment is enough
Listen to your friend's counsel before deciding
Go ahead quickly so doubts don't slow you down
Ask for advice only after the money is spent
items.explanation: Proverbs 12:15 says "The way of a fool is right in his own eyes: but he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise." The wise person listens to advice instead of trusting only their own view.
items.hint: Notice the contrast between someone sure of themselves and someone who listens.

items.prompt: During your annual review, you are tempted to spend the meeting listing all your accomplishments and describing yourself as the best performer on the team. Your manager has already noticed much of your work. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 27:2?
options: Praise yourself boldly, since no one else will speak up for you
Belittle your coworkers so your own work looks better
Answer honestly and let others, rather than your own mouth, do the praising
Post your achievements online so strangers will admire you
items.explanation: Proverbs 27:2 teaches, "Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth." Praise is fitting when it comes from others, not from self-promotion.
items.hint: The verse is about whose lips should speak your praise.

items.prompt: Your family is deciding whether to move across the country for a new job. You are inclined to make the decision alone so no one complicates things. What does Proverbs 15:22 counsel here?
options: Decide quietly by yourself, because more voices only cause confusion
Ask only one person who is sure to agree with you
Make the decision first and inform everyone afterward
Seek counsel from several wise, trusted people before deciding
items.explanation: Proverbs 15:22 says "Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established." Plans are made firm by seeking many wise advisers.
items.hint: The verse contrasts plans made with no input against plans made with many voices.

items.prompt: A colleague points out, privately and kindly, a serious error in a report you submitted. Your first instinct is to feel insulted and to avoid them. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 12:1?
options: Welcome the correction as a way to learn, rather than resenting it
Defend the report, since admitting fault damages your reputation
Report the colleague for overstepping
Ignore the feedback and wait for the issue to be forgotten
items.explanation: Proverbs 12:1 says "Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish." Loving correction is the path to knowledge, while hating it is called brutish.
items.hint: The verse describes the person who hates reproof in very unflattering terms.

items.prompt: At a neighborhood gathering, you notice yourself spending time only with the most successful and influential guests while ignoring a quiet newcomer who seems to be struggling. You also find yourself privately feeling smarter than most people there. What does Romans 12:16 counsel here?
options: Focus on networking with people who can raise your status
Associate with those of low estate and do not be wise in your own conceits
Keep your distance from the newcomer so you don't seem lowly
Trust your sense of superiority, since it reflects real wisdom
keywords: condescend to men of low estate
items.explanation: Romans 12:16 says "Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits." Believers are to associate with the lowly and avoid thinking too highly of their own wisdom.
items.hint: Paul addresses both who you spend time with and how you view your own wisdom.

items.prompt: You have led your department for twenty years. A young new hire respectfully suggests a better process, and you are tempted to dismiss it simply because of your seniority and long experience. Which response best reflects the teaching of Ecclesiastes 4:13?
options: Dismiss the idea, since age and position always outweigh youth
Accept advice only from people who are older than you
Stay teachable and open to admonition, regardless of your rank or age
Wait until the new hire has earned enough years before listening
items.explanation: Ecclesiastes 4:13 says "Better is a poor and a wise child than an old and foolish king, who will no more be admonished." Position and age are worth less than wisdom when a person refuses correction.
items.hint: The verse compares a young person and a ruler, and what makes the ruler foolish.

items.prompt: At a formal company dinner, you arrive early and are tempted to sit at the head table beside the CEO, even though no one has invited you there. What does Proverbs 25:6-7 counsel here?
options: Take the best seat early, since boldness gets you noticed
Sit near the CEO and wait to see whether anyone objects
Stand beside the important guests so you look important too
Take a modest place and let your host invite you higher
items.explanation: Proverbs 25:6-7 says "Put not forth thyself in the presence of the king," for it is better to be told "Come up hither" than to be put lower. Humbly waiting to be honored is better than being publicly demoted.
items.hint: The passage compares two ways of being moved by your host, one honorable and one embarrassing.

batch.theme: pride, humility, correction and seeking advice

items.prompt: Your sister calls, upset and accusing you of forgetting her birthday dinner. You feel unfairly blamed because the date was changed without telling you. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 15:1?
options: Answer her gently and calmly, acknowledging her hurt before explaining the mix-up
Raise your voice so she understands she is the one at fault
Point out sharply all the times she has forgotten your plans
Hang up and refuse to discuss it until she apologises
items.explanation: Proverbs 15:1 teaches that 'a soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger,' so a gentle reply is the wise path.
items.hint: The verse contrasts two kinds of words and what each one does to anger.

items.prompt: You and your spouse had a heated disagreement about household chores this evening. It is getting late, and you are tempted to go to bed still fuming and deal with it 'some other time.' What does Ephesians 4:26 counsel here?
options: Let the anger simmer for a few days so your spouse learns a lesson
Deal with the anger without sinning and seek to settle it before the day ends
Pretend nothing happened and never mention it again
Vent your frustration to friends instead of your spouse
keywords: sun go down upon your wrath
items.explanation: Ephesians 4:26 says, 'Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath,' urging that anger be resolved promptly rather than nursed.
items.hint: Think about what the verse says regarding the end of the day.

items.prompt: You are about to take part in a worship service when you remember that a close friend is still hurt by a careless remark you made last week. You would rather just focus on the service and let things blow over. What does Matthew 5:23-24 counsel here?
options: Carry on with your offering, since worship matters more than the friendship
Wait for your friend to come to you, since they are the one upset
First go and be reconciled with your friend, then come and offer your gift
Give a larger offering to make up for the remark
items.explanation: In Matthew 5:23-24 Jesus says to 'leave there thy gift before the altar' and 'first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.'
items.hint: Notice the order of actions Jesus gives in the passage.

items.prompt: A neighbour shares joyful news about her new grandchild, and later the same week another neighbour tells you his father has died. You are busy and tempted to keep your distance from both. Which response best reflects the teaching of Romans 12:15?
options: Stay neutral with both so you do not get too involved
Celebrate the good news but avoid the grieving neighbour to keep things positive
Remind the grieving neighbour that others have it worse
Share in the first neighbour's joy and grieve alongside the second
keywords: Rejoice with them that do rejoice
items.explanation: Romans 12:15 instructs, 'Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep,' calling us to share both the joys and sorrows of others.
items.hint: The verse names two emotions and asks you to share in each.

items.prompt: A friend once wronged a mutual acquaintance, apologised, and made it right. Now, in a group chat, someone asks whether you know anything about that old falling-out. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 17:9?
options: Let the settled matter rest rather than retelling it
Recount the full story so everyone has the facts
Hint at the details so people can guess what happened
Bring it up privately with each person in the group
items.explanation: Proverbs 17:9 says, 'He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends,' so repeating the old offence damages friendships.
items.hint: The proverb contrasts two responses to an offence and what each does to friendship.

items.prompt: A neighbour asks to borrow a tool you own and are not using; you could hand it over right now. You feel like saying, 'Come back tomorrow,' simply because it is inconvenient to dig it out. What does Proverbs 3:27-28 counsel here?
options: Tell him to come back another day, since your time is your own
Help him now, since it is in your power and you have it on hand
Refuse, because lending to neighbours always causes trouble
Promise to lend it but quietly hope he forgets
keywords: when thou hast it by thee
items.explanation: Proverbs 3:27-28 says, 'Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it,' and not to say 'to morrow I will give; when thou hast it by thee.'
items.hint: The passage warns against a particular kind of needless delay.

items.prompt: A crisis hits your household, and your nearest relative lives across the country. A longtime family friend and a nearby neighbour both offer immediate help, but you feel you should only rely on blood relatives. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 27:10?
options: Decline the friend's help, since only family should be trusted in hard times
Wait for your distant brother to travel to you before accepting any help
Value the faithful family friend and accept the near neighbour's help
Avoid involving anyone so you do not appear weak
keywords: better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off
items.explanation: Proverbs 27:10 says, 'Thine own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not,' and 'better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off.'
items.hint: The proverb compares the value of someone close at hand with a relative who is distant.

items.prompt: You want to thank a friend for a big favour, so you plan to show up at his door at dawn and loudly praise him before he has even woken up. You feel the enthusiasm proves your gratitude. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 27:14?
options: Go ahead, because louder praise always shows greater love
Praise him loudly in public so everyone hears how grateful you are
Repeat the early-morning praise several days in a row for emphasis
Consider his circumstances, since ill-timed, loud blessing can be received as a curse
items.explanation: Proverbs 27:14 warns, 'He that blesseth his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him,' so good intentions need wise timing.
items.hint: The proverb is about how and when a blessing is given, not just whether it is given.

items.prompt: You have a flexible remote job and no manager checking in daily. It's tempting to coast through the slow season and scramble later when the busy months arrive. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 6:6-8?
options: Relax fully now, since nobody is watching and the busy season is far off
Work steadily and prepare during the slow season, without needing someone to oversee you
Do only what is checked, because effort without a supervisor is wasted
Wait until the busy season starts and then decide how to cope
items.explanation: Proverbs 6:6-8 points the sluggard to the ant, which has "no guide, overseer, or ruler" yet "provideth her meat in the summer." Diligence and preparation should not depend on being supervised.
items.hint: Think of a small creature that gathers food before winter with no one telling it to.

items.prompt: You've been assigned a tedious task at work that your boss will probably never review closely. You're tempted to do the bare minimum since no one will notice the difference. What does Colossians 3:23 counsel here?
options: Do the bare minimum, since the effort will go unnoticed
Put in effort only when it will impress the people above you
Do the work wholeheartedly, as though doing it for the Lord rather than for people
Hand the task off to someone else, since unseen work doesn't matter
items.explanation: Colossians 3:23 says, "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." The quality of our work is not meant to depend on human recognition.
items.hint: The verse names a different audience for your work than your boss.

items.prompt: You're launching a small side project and have been anxiously drafting plans late into the night, relying entirely on your own cleverness. A friend suggests you approach the venture differently. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 16:3?
options: Commit your work to the LORD, trusting Him to establish your plans
Keep your plans to yourself, since sharing them invites failure
Abandon planning altogether and simply hope things work out
Rely solely on your own strategy, since success depends only on you
items.explanation: Proverbs 16:3 teaches, "Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established." Planning is paired with entrusting the work to God.
items.hint: The verse begins with an instruction about what to do with your works.

items.prompt: You're excited about a major home renovation and want to start knocking down walls this weekend. You haven't yet worked out whether you have the money to finish it. Which response best reflects Jesus' teaching in Luke 14:28-30?
options: Start right away; enthusiasm will carry the project to completion
Begin the demolition and figure out the budget once you see how it goes
Avoid all large projects, since any plan might fail
Sit down first and count the cost to see if you can finish what you start
items.explanation: In Luke 14:28-30 the builder of a tower "sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it." Otherwise onlookers mock the one who "began to build, and was not able to finish."
items.hint: Jesus describes someone building a tower and what he does before laying the foundation.

items.prompt: At dinner you confidently announce a five-year plan: move cities next spring, start a business, and be profitable within a year. A thoughtful friend gently questions how you're speaking about the future. Which response best reflects the teaching of James 4:13-15?
options: Speak of your plans humbly, saying, "If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that"
Make no plans at all, since planning is forbidden
Announce your plans boldly, since confidence guarantees success
Keep your plans vague so no one can hold you to them
items.explanation: James 4:13-15 reminds us that we "know not what shall be on the morrow" and that life is "a vapour," so we "ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that." James corrects presumption, not planning itself.
items.hint: James compares life to something that appears briefly and vanishes, then gives a phrase to add to our plans.

items.prompt: You're doing well in a steady job, and you've begun to think of your earnings purely as a means to upgrade your own lifestyle. A mentor asks you to consider a further purpose for your work. According to Ephesians 4:28, what is one stated purpose of honest labour?
options: To accumulate enough that you never need to work again
To have something to give to those in need
To earn status and recognition among peers
To prove you are more deserving than others
keywords: to give to him that needeth
items.explanation: Ephesians 4:28 urges honest work, "working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth." Labour is meant to provide for generosity, not only for self.
items.hint: The verse ends by naming someone who benefits from your work besides yourself.

items.prompt: For two years you've delayed starting a project, waiting for the economy, your schedule and your confidence to all line up perfectly. Each month you find a new reason the conditions aren't quite right. Which response best reflects the teaching of Ecclesiastes 11:4?
options: Keep waiting, because wise people act only when every condition is ideal
Recognize that endlessly watching for perfect conditions means you will never sow or reap
Give up on the project, since uncertain conditions prove it isn't meant to be
Let someone else decide for you so you are not responsible for the timing
items.explanation: Ecclesiastes 11:4 warns, "He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap." Waiting for perfect conditions leads to never acting at all.
items.hint: The verse pictures a farmer who keeps watching the weather.

items.prompt: A colleague urges you to rush into a quick-profit opportunity before thinking it through, promising fast results. You prefer to work out a careful, steady plan instead. What does Proverbs 21:5 contrast here?
options: It teaches that speed always beats careful thought in gaining wealth
It teaches that thinking about plans is pointless, since outcomes are random
It teaches that the diligent person's thoughts lead to plenty, while hastiness leads to want
It teaches that both haste and diligence lead to the same outcome
items.explanation: Proverbs 21:5 says, "The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want." Careful, diligent planning is contrasted with haste that ends in lack.
items.hint: The verse sets two kinds of people against each other: one careful, one in a hurry.

items.prompt: A routine medical test has you waiting a week for results, and you keep lying awake running through every possible outcome. A friend asks how you are holding up. Which response best reflects the teaching of Philippians 4:6-7?
options: Keep it to yourself, since bringing small worries to God would show a lack of faith
Bring your concerns to God in prayer with thanksgiving, trusting His peace to keep your heart and mind
Distract yourself completely and avoid thinking or praying about it until the week is over
Make anxiety your focus, since worrying hard shows you take the situation seriously
items.explanation: Paul writes, 'Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God,' promising that 'the peace of God' will keep hearts and minds (Philippians 4:6-7).
items.hint: Notice what Paul says to do 'in every thing' instead of being anxious.

items.prompt: Your manager hints that layoffs might come sometime next year. You start spending every evening imagining worst-case scenarios months ahead, and it is draining your joy today. What does Jesus counsel in Matthew 6:34?
options: Spend extra time each day rehearsing every possible future problem so nothing surprises you
Assume the worst will certainly happen and prepare to be miserable
Take no anxious thought for tomorrow; each day has enough trouble of its own
Worry now so that tomorrow will feel lighter
items.explanation: Jesus says, 'Take therefore no thought for the morrow... Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof' (Matthew 6:34), teaching His hearers not to borrow tomorrow's anxieties.
items.hint: Jesus says each day already carries enough of its own.

items.prompt: You are weighing two job offers. You have made spreadsheets and pro-and-con lists, and you are tempted to rely entirely on your own analysis without ever bringing the decision to God. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 3:5-6?
options: Trust the Lord with all your heart, not leaning on your own understanding, and acknowledge Him in the decision
Rely only on your own reasoning, since God is not concerned with everyday choices
Trust God with part of your heart while keeping the final say for your own wisdom
Acknowledge God only after the decision is made and has turned out well
items.explanation: Proverbs 3:5-6 says, 'Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.'
items.hint: The verse speaks of 'all thine heart' and 'all thy ways'.

items.prompt: A long, difficult season at home has tested you, and you are frustrated that it has not ended quickly. You find yourself asking whether hardship has any purpose at all. What does James 1:2-4 counsel here?
options: Treat every trial as proof that God has abandoned you
Try to escape the trial as fast as possible by any means, since it has no value
Count it joy, knowing the trying of your faith works patience that makes you mature
Pretend the difficulty is not real and refuse to acknowledge it
items.explanation: James writes, 'count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience,' and urges, 'let patience have her perfect work' (James 1:2-4).
items.hint: James connects testing with the growth of a particular virtue.

items.prompt: A coworker who cuts corners keeps getting praised and promoted while your honest work goes unnoticed. You feel bitterness rising and are tempted to bend the rules yourself. Which response best reflects the teaching of Psalms 37:7-8?
options: Start cutting corners too, since that is clearly what gets rewarded
Rest in the Lord and wait patiently, refusing to fret or let anger push you toward doing evil
Let your anger build until you can confront and expose him publicly
Conclude that honesty is pointless and give up trying to do right
items.explanation: The psalmist says, 'Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way... Cease from anger, and forsake wrath: fret not thyself in any wise to do evil' (Psalms 37:7-8).
items.hint: The psalm warns that fretting can lead somewhere worse.

items.prompt: You confidently announce to friends that next year you will move cities, start a business, and be turning a profit within twelve months. One friend gently asks how you are holding those plans before God. Which response best reflects the teaching of James 4:13-15?
options: Make plans humbly, recognizing life is like a vapour and saying, 'If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this'
Never make any plans at all, since planning is forbidden
Boast about the plans, since confidence guarantees success
Insist that your future is fully secure because you have worked out every detail
items.explanation: James notes 'ye know not what shall be on the morrow' and that life 'is even a vapour,' so 'ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that' (James 4:13-15).
items.hint: James does not condemn planning itself, but a certain attitude toward it.

items.prompt: You have wanted to start a volunteer ministry for years, but you keep postponing because the timing never feels perfect and you fear it might not succeed. Which response best reflects the teaching of Ecclesiastes 11:4-6?
options: Wait until every condition is ideal and success is certain before beginning
Give up the idea, since uncertainty means God is against it
Work only in the morning and stop if results do not come quickly
Stop waiting for perfect conditions and sow diligently, since you cannot know which effort will prosper
items.explanation: Ecclesiastes says 'He that observeth the wind shall not sow,' and counsels, 'In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper' (Ecclesiastes 11:4-6).
items.hint: Consider what happens to the farmer who keeps watching the weather.

items.prompt: A close friend calls you, weighed down with anxiety about family pressures. You are unsure whether to say anything or simply change the subject. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 12:25?
options: Avoid the topic entirely, since words make no difference to a heavy heart
Point out all the ways their situation could get even worse
Offer a good, encouraging word, because heaviness bows the heart but a good word makes it glad
Tell them their feelings are foolish and they should simply stop being anxious
keywords: a good word maketh it glad
items.explanation: Proverbs 12:25 observes, 'Heaviness in the heart of man maketh it stoop: but a good word maketh it glad,' showing the lifting power of kind, encouraging speech.
items.hint: The proverb contrasts what bows the heart with what gladdens it.

batch.theme: worry, fear, patience and trusting God

items.prompt: You are tempted to finance an expensive new car with a long, high-interest loan, even though your current car runs fine. A friend says the monthly payment is 'no big deal.' Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 22:7?
options: Take the loan, since debt has no real effect on your freedom
Remember that the borrower becomes servant to the lender, and weigh carefully before taking on debt you don't need
Borrow as much as possible now, because lenders work for borrowers
Ignore the cost entirely, since only the rich are affected by money matters
keywords: borrower is servant to the lender
items.explanation: Proverbs 22:7 says 'the borrower is servant to the lender,' warning that debt puts a person under another's power. Taking on unnecessary debt runs against this caution.
items.hint: Think about who holds power in a lending relationship.

items.prompt: Scrolling social media, you see friends showing off vacations and new homes, and you start feeling dissatisfied with your modest apartment. You catch yourself planning purchases just to keep up. What does Hebrews 13:5 counsel here?
options: Be content with what you have, trusting that God will never leave you
Keep up with others so you don't feel left behind
Envy is harmless as long as you don't say it out loud
Contentment only comes once you own as much as your neighbors
keywords: content with such things as ye have
items.explanation: Hebrews 13:5 urges, 'be content with such things as ye have,' grounding contentment in God's promise, 'I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.'
items.hint: The verse pairs a call to contentment with a promise of God's presence.

items.prompt: Your workplace is collecting donations for a coworker's family after a house fire. You feel pressured by a manager watching who gives, and you're tempted to give reluctantly just to look good. Which response best reflects the teaching of 2 Corinthians 9:7?
options: Give the largest amount so no one questions you
Give only because you were told you must
Decide in your heart what to give and give it cheerfully, not grudgingly
Give grudgingly, since the attitude doesn't matter as long as money is given
items.explanation: 2 Corinthians 9:7 says each should give 'as he purposeth in his heart... not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.' The heart behind the gift matters.
items.hint: The verse focuses on the giver's attitude more than the amount.

items.prompt: You've received a sizable bonus and are considering pouring all of it into luxury items. You realize your thoughts have been consumed by acquiring more possessions. Which response best reflects the teaching of Matthew 6:19-21?
options: Store up as many earthly goods as possible, since they last forever
Your heart and your treasure are unrelated, so spend however you like
Earthly possessions are safe from loss if you buy quality items
Lay up treasures in heaven rather than on earth, knowing your heart follows your treasure
items.explanation: Jesus teaches, 'lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven,' because earthly goods decay or are stolen, and 'where your treasure is, there will your heart be also' (Matthew 6:19-21).
items.hint: Consider what moth, rust, and thieves can and cannot reach.

items.prompt: A friend lent you money months ago and you now have enough in your account to repay it. You're tempted to tell them, 'Check back next month,' so you can enjoy a little extra cushion. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 3:27-28?
options: Delay repayment, since a friend should be patient indefinitely
Repay them now, since you have it and it is in your power to do good
Repay only if they ask several more times
Keep the money, since the loan was informal
keywords: when thou hast it by thee
items.explanation: Proverbs 3:27-28 says, 'Withhold not good from them to whom it is due,' and warns against saying 'to morrow I will give; when thou hast it by thee.'
items.hint: The passage specifically addresses putting someone off when you already have the means.

items.prompt: After a job loss, you've had to cut back sharply, and you feel your peace depends on your bank balance. You remember a time when money was plentiful and you felt no different inside. Which response best reflects the teaching of Philippians 4:11-12?
options: Learn to be content in every state, whether abased or abounding
Contentment is only possible when you have plenty
Contentment is only possible when you have very little
Paul teaches that circumstances must change before peace can come
items.explanation: Paul writes, 'I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content,' knowing both 'how to be abased' and 'how to abound' (Philippians 4:11-12). Contentment is learned, not dependent on circumstances.
items.hint: Paul says contentment is something he 'learned' across opposite situations.

items.prompt: In a moment of enthusiasm, you rashly pledged to stand behind an acquaintance's financial obligations, and now you realize you are bound by your own words. You're tempted to put off dealing with it. What does Proverbs 6:1-5 counsel here?
options: Relax and sleep on it for a few months; the situation will resolve itself
Take on additional pledges for others to show good faith
Act urgently and humbly, going to the person to seek to be released
Avoid the person entirely and hope they forget your promise
keywords: Give not sleep to thine eyes
items.explanation: Proverbs 6:1-5 says one who becomes 'surety for thy friend' is 'snared with the words of thy mouth' and should 'go, humble thyself,' giving 'not sleep to thine eyes' until delivered.
items.hint: The passage uses images of a roe and a bird escaping a hunter.

items.prompt: You're writing a personal prayer about your finances. Part of you wants to ask for great wealth, while another part fears hardship. Which request best reflects the prayer in Proverbs 30:8-9?
options: Ask for great riches, since abundance never draws the heart from God
Ask for poverty, since lack never tempts anyone to wrongdoing
Ask only for riches so that you never need to trust God
Ask for neither poverty nor riches, but enough, lest fullness lead to denying God or want lead to stealing
items.explanation: Proverbs 30:8-9 prays, 'give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me,' recognizing that being full may lead to denying God and being poor may lead to stealing.
items.hint: The writer sees spiritual danger at both extremes.

items.prompt: A coworker has openly mocked you in meetings and spread unkind rumors about you. A friend suggests you quietly return the favor or at least cut them off entirely. Which response best reflects the teaching of Matthew 5:44?
options: Love them, bless them, do good to them and pray for them
Ignore them completely until they apologize first
Gather evidence and expose their faults to the whole team
Return the treatment in kind so they learn a lesson
items.explanation: Jesus commands, "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them" (Matthew 5:44). Retaliation, exposure or cold withdrawal run against this command.
items.hint: Jesus lists four active things to do toward those who mistreat you.

items.prompt: You help greet people at a community gathering. A well-dressed businessman and a visibly poor man in worn clothes arrive at the same time, and you feel tempted to give the businessman the best seat. What does James 2:1-4 counsel here?
options: Seat the businessman up front, since he may support the group
Ask the poor man to stand at the back so others feel comfortable
Show no partiality, welcoming both with equal honor
Let the poor man in only if there are seats left over
items.explanation: James warns against holding the faith "with respect of persons," rebuking those who honor the man with the gold ring while telling the poor man in vile raiment, "Stand thou there" (James 2:1-4).
items.hint: James describes this exact seating situation and calls favoritism being partial.

items.prompt: A struggling neighbor asks for help buying groceries this week. You hesitate, thinking you'll never get the money back. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 19:17?
options: Refuse, because money given away is simply lost
Help only if the neighbor signs a promise to repay
Give with pity, trusting that kindness to the poor is lent to the LORD
Tell the neighbor to rely on someone wealthier
items.explanation: Proverbs 19:17 says, "He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again." Giving to the needy is not lost but entrusted to God.
items.hint: The verse describes generosity to the poor as a kind of loan, but not to the poor person.

items.prompt: A former friend who betrayed you is now going through hard times and is short on food. You learn they are hungry and could easily help. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 25:21-22?
options: Wait and let them experience the consequences of their choices
Give them food and drink, trusting the LORD to reward you
Help only after they publicly admit what they did
Tell mutual friends so everyone knows they deserve it
items.explanation: Proverbs 25:21-22 instructs, "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink," adding that "the LORD shall reward thee."
items.hint: The passage names both hunger and thirst and tells you what to do about each.

items.prompt: A relative cheated you in a family business deal and you are furious. You are considering ways to make them pay without anyone knowing it was you. Which response best reflects the teaching of Romans 12:17-19?
options: Repay them quietly in a way that matches the harm they caused
Refuse to repay evil for evil, seek peace where possible, and leave vengeance to God
Take revenge only if you are certain they are guilty
Cut off all contact and warn others to punish them socially
items.explanation: Paul writes, "Recompense to no man evil for evil... live peaceably with all men. Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves... Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Romans 12:17-19).
items.hint: The passage explains who is to repay wrongs.

items.prompt: A family from another country moves into your neighborhood. Some neighbors are cool toward them and make jokes about their accent and customs. Which response best reflects the teaching of Leviticus 19:33-34?
options: Keep your distance until they adapt to local ways
Join the jokes lightly so you fit in with your neighbors
Treat them as one born among you and love them as yourself
Be polite but make clear they are guests, not equals
items.explanation: Leviticus 19:33-34 commands, "Ye shall not vex him. But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself."
items.hint: The passage reminds Israel that they themselves were once strangers in Egypt.

items.prompt: You hired a day laborer to do yard work. The job is done, but it would be more convenient to pay him at the end of the month with your other bills. Which response best reflects the teaching of Deuteronomy 24:14-15?
options: Pay him the same day, before the sun goes down, since he depends on it
Pay at month's end; any delay is fine as long as you pay eventually
Reduce his pay since he is poor and will accept less
Pay him only if he reminds you several times
items.explanation: Deuteronomy 24:14-15 says not to oppress a poor hired servant: "At his day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it."
items.hint: The passage gives a specific time limit tied to the day's end.

items.prompt: A rival at work who treated you unfairly has just been publicly reprimanded and demoted. Colleagues invite you to celebrate their downfall over lunch. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 24:17-18?
options: Celebrate, since justice has finally been done
Smile inwardly but avoid saying anything publicly
Refuse to rejoice in their fall, guarding even your heart from gladness at it
Remind everyone of what they did so the lesson sticks
items.explanation: Proverbs 24:17-18 warns, "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth," because it displeases the LORD. This covers inward gladness, not just outward celebration.
items.hint: The verse addresses not only your words but also your heart.

batch.theme: justice, kindness to the poor, strangers and enemies
